one_liner: Single-node Go AMQP 0.9.1 broker speaking RabbitMQ's wire protocol; author measures 1.1-4.5x RabbitMQ 4.3's durable, confirmed throughput.
what_it_does: A standalone AMQP 0.9.1 server that existing RabbitMQ client libraries (amqp091-go, pika, amqplib, the Java and .NET clients, bunny) connect to without code changes. You can run it as one static binary, or embed it in a Go program with server.NewServerBuilder().WithConfig(cfg).Build() followed by Start(); an embedded broker still serves clients over TCP. It covers direct/fanout/topic/headers exchanges, exchange-to-exchange bindings, publisher confirms, transactions, basic.get/return/recover, TTLs, dead-lettering, max-length/overflow, TLS/mTLS, SASL PLAIN/ANONYMOUS, per-vhost permissions, Prometheus metrics and pprof. It is not a full RabbitMQ replacement: there is no clustering or HA and no management UI.
how_it_is_fast: All queues share one write-ahead log whose writer goroutine does drain-then-flush group commit: every record that queued up while the previous fsync ran (up to 1000) goes out in one write and one fdatasync (Linux) or os.File.Sync (other OSes), and a publish is confirmed only after its batch is synced. Confirms are batched too: each channel tracks a contiguous durable watermark with atomics, and a per-connection flusher sends a single basic.ack with multiple=true for the whole range. Each queue keeps an in-memory ring of message pointers where the slot is the delivery tag masked to the ring size, claimed with a per-slot CAS (64K slots by default); messages spill to the WAL at 80% full and are later checkpointed to segment files. On the connection side, separate reader/processor goroutines and a dedicated ack goroutine feed batched deliveries that go out as one write per batch (writev for bodies of 32 KB or more), with frames pooled via sync.Pool.
when_to_use: Go services or CI suites that need a real AMQP 0.9.1 broker without an Erlang runtime or Docker: embed it in the process or ship one static binary (release builds exist for linux-386/amd64/arm64 and darwin-amd64/arm64).

Single-node, durable, publisher-confirm workloads where many producers feed one queue with small (~1 KB) messages. In the author's table StrangeQ holds about 107-114K msg/s at 10-30 producers, while RabbitMQ's default classic queue drops to about 24-25K.

Integration tests for code written against RabbitMQ clients, where a quick-starting in-process broker matters more than full RabbitMQ feature parity. The repo has a conformance target (make conformance-rabbitmq) that checks behavior against RabbitMQ 4.3.
Teams that want to profile and debug the broker with standard Go tools (net/http/pprof, go tool pprof) and scrape Prometheus metrics, instead of using Erlang tooling.
when_not_to_use: Anything that needs clustering, replication or HA; the README lists these as not implemented. It does not mention quorum queues, streams, or plugins such as shovel or federation.
Apps that depend on priority queues (x-max-priority), consumer priorities, lazy queues, global QoS, prefetch_size > 0 (rejected with 540), SASL EXTERNAL, connection.secure, or the management UI/CLI.
Large-message workloads: with 64 KB bodies the author's lead shrinks to 1.10x.

Production systems where the durability track record matters. The Show HN says an LLM wrote the code; it has one maintainer, 5 stars and no third-party bug reports. Fixes for a WAL read-path deadlock and for acknowledged records being served again from the segment tier landed in August 2026, after the benchmark was run.

Code that relies on RabbitMQ edge semantics the README lists as divergent. Zero-TTL messages are dropped when no consumer is ready. A malformed per-message expiration is treated as no TTL. reject-publish is not enforced inside a transaction. A mandatory publish to a full reject-publish queue is returned with code 312.

integration.form: module (Go module github.com/maxpert/amqp-go in src/amqp-go of the strangeq repo; also prebuilt server binaries)
integration.dependencies: go.uber.org/zap, knadh/koanf (yaml/env/file), prometheus/client_golang, RoaringBitmap/roaring, fxamacker/cbor, HdrHistogram/hdrhistogram-go, golang.org/x/crypto, x/sys, x/sync, gopkg.in/yaml.v3 (plus rabbitmq/amqp091-go for perftest/tests and stretchr/testify for tests)
integration.platforms: Linux (uses fdatasync) and macOS (uses os.File.Sync). Release binaries cover linux-386/amd64/arm64 and darwin-amd64/arm64. There are Windows-specific source files but no Windows release binary.
integration.thread_safety: The broker is internally concurrent: separate reader and processor goroutines per connection, a dedicated ack goroutine, and one shared WAL writer goroutine. Thread-safety of the embedding API is not documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — AMQP 0.9.1 clients connect unchanged to a single node, but there is no clustering/HA, priority queues, consumer priorities, lazy queues, global QoS, SASL EXTERNAL or management UI/CLI, and the README documents a few behavioral divergences

gotchas: The module path in go.mod (github.com/maxpert/amqp-go) does not match the repo, and proxy.golang.org returns 'not found' for it. So the README's `go install github.com/maxpert/amqp-go/cmd/amqp-server@latest` and plain library imports do not resolve: clone and build in src/amqp-go, or use a replace directive.

The latest release, v0.10.0 (2026-07-02), predates both the benchmarked build (measured 2026-07-14) and the August 2026 data-loss and deadlock fixes. Build from main if you want the benchmarked and fixed code.

The WAL format v4 is a deliberate clean break: files from older versions are rejected with ErrUnsupportedWALVersion. The --unsafe-recovery flag lets the broker start but discards the unparseable file, so drain queues before upgrading across formats.

The README says a bare `amqp-server` runs 'in-memory', but DefaultConfig writes to ./data with fsync and per-record CRC32 turned on (the sample config puts the CRC cost at about 8% CPU; fsync:false is an opt-in that transactions ignore). Each queue keeps unacked messages in its RAM ring (64K slots by default, 262144 in the README's production example) and spills to the WAL at 80% full.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick StrangeQ when you want an AMQP 0.9.1 broker you can embed in a Go program; it is the only catalogued sibling benchmarked directly against RabbitMQ 4.3 on durable, confirmed traffic. Prefer LavinMQ (AMQP 0-9-1 plus MQTT, about 1K stars, actively developed) when maturity matters, and skip SocketPro if you must keep AMQP clients, since its RabbitMQ win comes from its own C++ framework (repo last pushed 2023).
verified_claims_summary: On one 16-core Apple Silicon Mac (chip model and Go version not stated), the author ran RabbitMQ 4.3 (default classic queue, in an OrbStack ARM64 Linux container; the README does not say whether the container's fsyncs reach the host disk) and host-native StrangeQ under the same amqp091-go perftest: one durable queue, persistent 1 KB messages, confirms with up to 1000 in flight per producer, fsync on, prefetch 100, 20 s runs, median per-second consumed rate. StrangeQ was 1.67x RabbitMQ at 1 producer/1 consumer and about 4.4x at 10/10 and 30/30, mostly because RabbitMQ fell from 64.5K to about 25K msg/s while StrangeQ stayed at 107-114K; with 64 KB bodies it was 1.10x.
status_note: Actively developed by one maintainer (last commit 2026-08-29, many July-August commits fixing races, deadlocks and a data-loss path) and MIT-licensed, but it has 5 stars, no outside issues, and a latest release older than the fixes: fine for tests and experiments, unproven in production.
